content: Certainly. 1. Changes in weight, depression, dizziness, headache, nervousness, somnolence, breast tenderness, galactorrhea, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, and cholestatic jaundice are potential side effects associated with estrogen and progestin therapy. 2. Serious complications such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT), thrombophlebitis, endometrial hyperplasia, endocervical polyps, uterine leiomyomata, fallopian tube cysts, uterine spasms, and breast cancer have been reported. 3. Hypertension, varicose veins, jaundice, cholestatic jaundice, cholelithiasis, gallbladder disorders, and increased transaminase levels may occur with estrogen use. 4. Skin discoloration, mood instability, libido disorders, migraines, vertigo, paresthesia, angioedema, and hypersensitivity reactions (including anaphylaxis or angioedema) have been observed. 5. Estrogen and progestin therapy is contraindicated in individuals with known protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiencies, or other thrombophilic disorders, as well as in pregnancy, estrogen-dependent neoplasia, or a history of DVT/PE, arterial thromboembolic disease, breast cancer, or liver disease/tumors. 6. Unexplained abnormal vaginal bleeding should be evaluated before initiating therapy. Caution is advised in patients with changes in bone mineral density, a history of depression, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, obesity, endometriosis, a family history of breast cancer or DVT/PE, smoking, epilepsy, migraines, or renal/cardiac impairment. 7. Estrogen therapy should be discontinued if DVT/PE, stroke, myocardial infarction (MI), jaundice, visual disturbances, or severe migraines occur. Therapy should also be stopped 4-6 weeks before major surgery or during prolonged immobilization. 8. The Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) estrogen plus progestin study reported an increased risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) events, particularly in the first year of therapy, with a trend toward decreasing risk in subsequent years. The estrogen-alone study showed no overall effect on CHD events. 9. Estrogen therapy may increase the risk of postoperative thromboembolic complications. Discontinuation 4-6 weeks before major surgery or during periods of prolonged immobilization is recommended. 10. Migraine with aura has been reported with estrogen therapy. In some epidemiologic studies, long-term use (≥5 years) of estrogen plus progestin or estrogen-only products has been associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer, though findings are inconsistent across studies. 11. Estrogen therapy may cause severe hypercalcemia in patients with breast cancer and bone metastases. If hypercalcemia occurs, therapy should be discontinued, and appropriate measures should be taken to lower serum calcium levels. 12. Angioedema involving the eyes, eyelids, face, larynx, pharynx, tongue, and extremities (hands, legs, ankles, and fingers) has been reported. Women who develop angioedema during treatment should not receive estrogen therapy again. Exogenous estrogens may exacerbate symptoms in women with hereditary angioedema. 13. Anaphylactic or anaphylactoid reactions requiring emergency medical management have been reported. Estrogen therapy may elevate plasma triglycerides in women with preexisting hypertriglyceridemia, potentially leading to pancreatitis. Discontinuation should be considered if pancreatitis occurs. 14. Transdermal estrogen therapy avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism but may still be poorly metabolized in women with impaired liver function. Caution is advised in women with a history of cholestatic jaundice associated with past estrogen use or pregnancy. Therapy should be discontinued if jaundice recurs. 15. Estrogen therapy increases thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels, potentially necessitating higher doses of thyroid hormone replacement therapy in dependent women. Thyroid function should be monitored to maintain free thyroid hormone levels within an acceptable range. 16. Estrogen plus progestin therapy may cause fluid retention, which can exacerbate conditions such as cardiac or renal impairment, asthma, migraines, epilepsy, or systemic lupus erythematosus. Therapy should be discontinued if medically concerning fluid retention occurs. 17. Estrogen therapy should be used cautiously in women with hypoparathyroidism, as it may induce hypocalcemia. In women with residual endometriosis post-hysterectomy, the addition of progestin should be considered to mitigate the risk of malignant transformation of residual endometrial implants. 18. Estrogen therapy may exacerbate asthma, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, migraines, porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas. The risks and benefits of therapy should be carefully weighed in such cases. 19. Risk factors for arterial vascular disease (e.g., hypertension, diabetes mellitus, tobacco use, hypercholesterolemia, and obesity) and venous thromboembolism (e.g., personal or family history of VTE, obesity, and systemic lupus erythematosus) should be managed appropriately. 20. Estrogen therapy is not recommended in conditions predisposing to hyperkalemia. Postmenopausal women receiving estrogen therapy have a 2to 4-fold increased risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery. 21. Retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogen therapy. Therapy should be discontinued if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision, proptosis, diplopia, or migraines. If papilledema or retinal vascular lesions are detected, estrogen therapy should not be resumed. 22. Progestins combined with estrogens may have adverse effects on lipoprotein metabolism (e.g., lowering HDL and raising LDL) and impair glucose tolerance. Observational studies have reported an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy and a smaller risk with estrogen-alone therapy after several years of use. 23. Women should undergo annual breast examinations by a healthcare provider and perform monthly breast self-examinations. Mammography should be scheduled based on age, risk factors, and prior results. Estrogen therapy has been associated with an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation. 24. Estrogen therapy is not indicated during pregnancy. While epidemiologic studies and meta-analyses have not shown an increased risk of birth defects with combined hormonal contraceptives, estrogen plus progestogens are present in human milk and may reduce milk production in breastfeeding women. 25. Estradiol, an endogenous estrogen, reduces the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus and decreases the secretion of LH and FSH from the pituitary gland. It also increases the synthesis of DNA, RNA, and proteins in target tissues. 26. Norethindrone acetate, a progestin, inhibits gonadotropin secretion from the pituitary gland, preventing follicular maturation and ovulation while stimulating mammary tissue growth. 27. Estradiol has a peak plasma time of 5-8 hours (oral administration), while norethindrone peaks at 1-2 hours (oral administration). Estradiol is 98% protein-bound, and norethindrone is 90-97% protein-bound. Bioavailability is approximately 50% for estradiol and 100% for norethindrone. 28.
